entries.description:
Runs a query from code and answers with an ordinary QueryResult. The source is one of two things, told apart by whitespace. A registered source written `Kind.Name` — `Catalog.Goods`, `Document.Invoice`, `AccumulationRegister.Stock` — and the composer writes the query over it itself, reading every field the source has. Or the text of a query: anything with a space or a line break in it is text, and it is run as written.

The result is walked exactly like the one `New Query(text).Execute()` gives. QueryText shows the text that runs — the way to see what a source turns into. Parameters (`&Name` in the text) are given with SetParameter before Execute.

With no source the composer is empty: QueryText answers "" and Execute an empty result. A name with no dot and no space is read as text, and the query's parser refuses it when it runs.
entries.parameters: source — `Kind.Name` of a registered source, or the text of a query (it contains a space or a line break).

entries.description: Gives the query's parameter `&name` its value. It stays for every later Execute of this composer; setting the same name again replaces it. A name the query does not use is simply not asked for.
entries.parameters:
name — the parameter's name as the text writes it after `&`, without the `&`.
value — its value.

entries.description: Runs the query — the one written over the source, or the text as given — and answers with a QueryResult, the same kind `New Query(text).Execute()` gives: walked with Select, read the same way. A query the engine cannot read raises with the engine's own message. An empty composer answers with an empty result.

The text of the query the composer runs, without running it. For a source it is the query written over it — `SELECT <every field of the source> FROM <source>`; for a text, that text. Paste it into a Query when something has to be looked at by hand. An empty composer answers "".
entries.example:
Message(New DataComposer("AccumulationRegister.Stock").QueryText());
// SELECT Active, Period, RecordType, Recorder, LineNumber, Item, Warehouse, Quantity FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock

entries.description:
A report's data: the query it reads and what its settings say about filtering, sorting, grouping and totals. A report object has one for every composer it declares, under the composer's name (`Object.Main`, read-only); a composer template under any other object is taken with GetTemplate(name), which hands out a composition of its own. A form attribute may hold one too — the grid box bound to it shows the report.

A script composes it as it stands: Compose writes the result into a SpreadsheetDocument, Refresh builds the report again into the sheet the composition holds. What it reads and how it folds it — query, parameters, resources, groupings, variants — is set in the designer and in the settings window. Its parameters are worked out when it runs, expressions among them evaluated at that moment, so `CurrentDate()` means the day the report is built.

`New DataComposition()` makes an empty one: with no query, composing it raises.

Runs the composition and writes the report into the given document — the heading, the column titles, the rows, the groupings as row groups — with the settings in force at this moment. The document is the caller's: show it, print it, put it into another one.

A query the engine could not read raises with the engine's own message, rather than leaving an empty sheet nobody can explain; so does a composition with no query at all. A report that found no rows is an empty report, not an error. Anything other than a SpreadsheetDocument is refused.
entries.parameters: document — the SpreadsheetDocument to write into.

entries.description: Builds the report again, with whatever its settings now say, into the sheet the composition itself holds — the one a grid box bound to it shows. Compose is the verb for a document of your own; Refresh is the report form's "generate" said from code.

entries.signature: New CompositionField(path : string, presentation : string = path)
entries.description:
One field of a source, held as a value: `Supplier.Region` is a path, and this is the field it names. A list's and a report's settings point at fields this way — the left side of a filter line, a sort line, a grouping level.

Two CompositionFields are equal when their paths are, regardless of case; a field is never equal to a string, even one that spells its path. Its string is the presentation, or the path when it has none. A field made in a script carries no type: it learns it from the source it is used with.
entries.parameters:
path — the field's path in the source's names, dot-separated.
presentation — what a person reads instead of the path; left out, the path is shown.

entries.description: The field's path, dot-separated, in the source's names. Written, it points the value at another field — and the type the old field carried is dropped, to be learnt again from the source.
What a person reads for the field. Read, it answers in the reader's language when it was written in several, and with the path when there is no presentation; written, it is kept as given.

One of the values a configuration declares — a predefined item of a catalog, say — held as a name rather than read: which object, which of its declared values, and the text it was chosen as (`CatalogRef.Goods.Chair`). A composition's settings hold one where the designer chose a declared value for a parameter or a filter, and it becomes the live reference when the composition runs. An empty reference of a type is a value it can hold.

A SCRIPT NEVER MAKES ONE — `New CompositionPredefinedValue()` does not compile — and it has no members; its string is the text it was chosen as.

How a filter line of a list or a report compares its field — what the comparison cell of a filter line offers. A line means the same however it is answered: in the query the composer writes, or over rows already read. Filled and NotFilled take no value: they ask only whether the field holds one.

A script names a member as ComparisonKind.<Name>.
The field equals the value. The default for a new line.
The field differs from the value.
The field is greater than the value.
The field is less than the value.
The field is greater than the value or equal to it.
The field is less than the value or equal to it.
The field's text contains the value anywhere in it — a LIKE with the value between `%` wildcards. The value is not escaped, so a `%` or `_` in it is a wildcard too.
The field equals one of the values — a list of them (an Array, a ValueList and the like), or a single value, which stands for itself.
The field is one of the values or lies anywhere beneath one of them in its hierarchy — a folder and everything in it, at every depth. One value or a list of them, as for In.
The field holds a value: neither NULL nor the empty value of its type (an empty reference, "", 0, an empty date, False). The line takes no value of its own.
The field holds no value: NULL — a row that has no such field at all — or the empty value of its type. On screen both are an empty cell, so they are one question. The line takes no value of its own.

Which way a sort line of a list or a report orders its field.

A script names a member as SortDirection.<Name>.
Smallest first. The default.
Largest first.

How a grouping level unfolds a field that has a hierarchy — a catalog with folders. The same three words the query language says (`TOTALS ... BY Item HIERARCHY`), so a report, a filter and a query mean the same thing by them. A field with no hierarchy groups by its values whichever is chosen.

A script names a member as GroupKind.<Name>.
The values themselves, each a group of its own, with nothing above them — the folders they stand in are not shown. The default.
The values arranged in their hierarchy: every folder as a group with its total, and the elements inside it.
The folders alone: each with the total of everything under it, the elements counted but not shown as groups of their own.

How a group of filter lines joins the lines under it. A filter is a tree: the lines stand in groups, and a group can hold groups, which is how "this AND (that OR the other)" is said. The filter itself is the outer group, an And unless set otherwise.

A script names a member as FilterGroupKind.<Name>.
Every line of the group holds. The default.
At least one line of the group holds.
The lines of the group do not all hold together: NOT of their And.

Where a person meets a filter line. It changes what is offered, never what is applied: the line filters the same way in every mode.

A script names a member as FilterDisplayMode.<Name>.
In the settings window. The default.
In the settings window and also beside the data, in the list's header — for the filters people change every day.
Applied and never shown: the person can neither see the line nor change it.

A list read from the base page by page — what a list form shows. It stands on a MAIN TABLE (a catalog, a document, a register), which says whose rows they are and what can be done with one: open it, create one, mark it for deletion. A query of its own, when it has one, changes what is read over that table, not whose rows they are. Its filter, sort and grouping are its settings, edited in its settings window and by the person in the list.

A script meets one as a form attribute — a generated list form names its main attribute `List` — or as the Value of a table box. It asks two things of it: Refresh to read again, GetMetadata for what it lists. The current row of a table box showing it is a DynamicListRow.

`New DynamicList()` makes an empty one, with no main table.
entries.example: List.Refresh();   // in the list form's module: read the rows again

entries.description: Reads the list again: its settings as they now stand are applied and every row is fetched anew, so rows written since appear and removed ones go. The table box showing it follows.

The metadata object of the list's main table — the catalog, document or register whose rows it lists; its properties (Name and the rest) are read as any metadata object's. A list with no main table — one made with `New DynamicList()` — answers Undefined.

One row of a dynamic list as a script holds it — the current row of a table box that shows the list (`Controls.Table1.CurrentRow`). Its fields are the list's columns, read by name: the main table's fields and those its query adds. A row is read, not written: the list shows the base, and a change goes through the object the row stands for.

A script never makes one. Writing a reference into the table box's CurrentRow puts it on that object's row.
